newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht - First estimate of European beet areas.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht - First estimate of European beet areas.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
FIRST ESTIMATE OF EUROPEAN SUGAR BEET AREAS 1997

(All figures in 1,000 ha. First figure 1997, second figure 1996) Austria 51/52, Belgium 101/104, Denmark 65/68, Finland 34/34, France 420/425, Germany 514/515, Greece 50/40, Ireland 33/34, Italy 275/248, Netherlands 115/117, Portugal 2/2, Spain 155/160, Sweden 60/59, UK 170/170.

Switzerland 17/17, Turkey 450/416, ex Yugoslavia 100/105, West Europe total 2,612/2,566, Czech Republic 95/94, Slovakia 47/43, Hungary 102/115, Poland 380/451, Romania 165/137, Russia 1,080/1,071, Ukraine 1,350/1,418.

Europe is an important factor in the world sugar market. Not only are many of its countries exporters of white sugar but several of them are also major importers of both raw and white sugar. Early indications of sowings intentions in the continent are therefore of considerable importance to the market.

The area sown to sugar beet in Western Europe this year is expected to be slightly higher than in 1996. In the EU it was at first expected that the area in France would be higher but the surplus of sugar brought forward from last season combined with lower world market prices appear to have discouraged farmers and sowings are now expected to fall somewhat below last season's area. In Germany, on the other hand, the area is expected to remain largely unchanged.

In the UK the area tends to be stable from year to year and once again no change is anticipated. There was a dramatic fall in sowings in Italy last year due to a change in pricing arrangements but a significant recovery can be expected in 1997. The other two EU members producing in excess of one mn tonnes of sugar - Spain and the Netherlands - are both expecting small declines in area. Production of sugar is expected to rise in Turkey in 1997/98, though growers have made it clear they will need a large price increase for their beet.

Planting started early in Serbia this year and the government has set a target of 100,000 ha. However, 60/70,000 ha is thought to be a more likely figure. Taking the countries of Western Europe as a group it seems likely that there will be a modest overall increase in the area sown to the crop this year.

Several of the governments of Eastern European countries have yet to rid themselves of the practice of setting unrealistic plans and this makes forecasting somewhat difficult. Leaving aside official figures, a slight rise in area is expected in the Russian Federation this year, but this will be more than counterbalanced by a drop in the Ukraine.

A surplus of sugar was produced in Poland in 1996/97 and part of this will either have to be exported at a loss or brought forward to the current year. Consequently sowings are expected to fall this year. Hungary also produced a surplus and here too, a drop in sowing is anticipated. On the other hand, though more sugar was produced in the Czech Republic last year than was required for domestic needs, it is thought likely that the area will be slightly increased this year.

Slovakia, which is a sugar importer, is also expected to increase its beet area slightly. Taken as a group it seems likely that there will not be any great change in the total area sown to beet in Eastern Europe; if anything, the area may be slightly down.

Though the area in Western Europe may be up in 1997 this need not mean that sugar output will rise as last year yields got a late boost from favourable autumn weather. Based upon more normal weather this year and currently anticipated sowings output in Western Europe might be expected to fall by nearly 900,000 tonnes. The reverse was true in Eastern Europe last season; adverse weather was reflected in sugar yields last year and a return to more normal conditions could prevent any major fall in output. Accordingly, despite the expected fall in area, output might not be greatly changed.

Though current indications may suggest that European sugar production will show a high degree of stability, it must never be overlooked that we are dealing with an agricultural crop that can be greatly affected by weather conditions.
